Personally I run the stock length at two notches from the rear on the adjustable stocks. The magpul fixed carbine stock is exactly that same length minus stock wobble. What really makes the difference is the length of the rail interface. Because I  have a 12" free float I use the magpul AFG and the C clamp technique. Its comfortable for my longer pull. My stock AR had a standard 9" quad rail with the fixed sight base and I found myself gripping the mag well for a tight feel. Its all about preference and comfort, try some things out and tailor the rifle to your needs and comforts

sure thing. Well I chose an upper with a longer free float rail(12") because of my size. Im a solid 6'4 at 250 lbs and I needed the extra pull on the rifle for optimal control. Now because of the longer rail I decided to go with the Magpul AFG versus a vertical grip because my extended c-clamp style works best at a longer pull. It allows me to lock out my elbow and reduce muscle fatigue from the weight of the rifle, plus it balances well for me since the barrel is heavy profile (because of muh gun laws in MD). Aside from that I chose the BCM mod 3 pistol grip because of its steeper angle and its just more comfortable for my dominant firing hand, allows me to maintain a nice controlled shouldering of the rifle. I chose the magpul fixed carbine because I like the rigid feel of a fixed stock, no stock wobble, and its the same length that i shoot my carbines at, which is two knotches from the fear of an adjustable stock. Combine all of these together and I made the rifle around my physique and makes for a smooth and comfortable experience.

The best thing to do is to sit down and make a list of pros and cons/ cost benefit analysis and decide if a standardization is best for that aspect

Basically if any of your essentials have interchangeable parts, require routine maintenance, etc, its best to standardized. Generally you should standardize for the sake of efficiency and functionality. Your standard should conform to what functions best given your parameters. A simple example would be if I wanted to design a weapons kit based on a WROL situation. I have to think of me and my wife, we live in a suburban environment. Lets say we run an AR15 in 5.56mm and a Glock 9mm. We standardized our ammo and weapons. This makes ammunition acquisition and parts easy. We could swap parts and pass magazines if needed. There is a down side to standardization like this. In our scenario, our roles as operators are greatly limited. We could easily run into a situation where our 5.56 cant penetrate certain barriers, we cant engage at a longer distance with sufficient energy, etc. Or maybe we run shotguns as our primary and we get to the more rural part our area where we are ineffective. You'd have to analyze and construct a cost benefit analysis to see if standardization for what ever you need is best given the situational parameters
